text: Every enforcement point this chapter has relied on so far assumed some control over the network path or the infrastructure involved. A SaaS application breaks that assumption completely — the vendor hosts it, the vendor's infrastructure enforces access to it, and your policy enforcement points have no path to intercept traffic between a browser and that vendor's servers at all.

Employees and departments adopt dozens to hundreds of SaaS tools over time, often without IT ever provisioning or knowing about them. That unmanaged layer is shadow IT, and nearly every SaaS security program starts by discovering how large it actually is — you can't apply any zero-trust control to an application nobody even registered.

A cloud access security broker inserts itself into the path between users and SaaS apps, either as a proxy traffic routes through or via API integrations with the vendor's own management APIs. From there it extends the same DLP and conditional-access policies this course covered for first-party apps — blocking a restricted file upload, or requiring step-up authentication on a risky sign-in.

A CASB mostly governs the path to the app. SaaS security posture management looks inward at the app's own configuration instead — continuously checking a connected tenant for an open public sharing link, an admin account missing MFA, or an OAuth app granted far more scope than it needs. These are settings a traffic-path control would never see.

Conditional access still extends past apps you built, because federated SaaS sign-in routes through your own identity provider, letting the same device and risk checks apply to a third-party app's sign-in. And every OAuth 'Allow' click creates a long-lived integration that needs that same governance and auditing.
That closes Chapter 5. Chapter 6 picks up from here, turning everything built across these five lessons into a measurable zero-trust maturity model you can actually score.
